proof.criterion: Tester's failure 1: the per-address reread limit must be derived from the shared bucket the process actually mounts, so no single unauthenticated address can hold the fleet's reread budget at zero and no deployment is tightened by a bucket it does not mount.
proof.surface: The tester's own red row, which mounts a 1 s shared bucket and a 4 s one through api.Register's real mux and reads the refusing bucket's rate out of the 429's Retry-After header. It is blind to where the factor comes from, so it stays red if the derivation is ever dropped.
proof.observed: Both subtests PASS: 1s in 0.55 s and 4s in 0.34 s. DefaultRereadLimit is deleted outright, with no shim and no alias; the per-address limit is RereadLimitFor(overall) = {Every: perAddressFactor (2) x overall.Every, Burst: DefaultRereadBurst (30)}, derived in Register after the shared bucket is resolved and only when the caller passed none, so the two rows that inject their own per-address bucket keep driving it. An AWS process therefore gets one every 2 s — exactly what it had before this issue — and a Secret Manager process one every 8 s, with the ordering (at least two addresses to starve the fleet) identical on both stores. grep finds no DefaultRereadLimit anywhere in packages/envoy.
proof.negativeControl: The tester drove the failure on the real binary before this push: an aws-secrets-manager broker accepted 33 rereads from one address and then answered Retry-After: 8 from that address's own bucket, against a shared bucket whose own refusals carried Retry-After: 1 — an eighth of the bucket it mounts instead of a half. The row is unmodified: jj diff --from 3b4e444c9cb1 over handlers_secrets_test.go shows one hunk, a stale burst figure in an unrelated comment, and the row itself is byte-identical.

proof.criterion: Tester's failure 2: the burst rule walked the depth under the floor its own guard enforces, and the floor was stated lower than the measured one — both wrong in the direction that makes a change look safe.
proof.surface: The repository's end-to-end row for the real client (cmd/agent-secrets), which drives the compiled CLI against a real broker rig on a real Postgres and mounts no bucket of its own.
proof.observed: ok in 0.51 s. Both shared buckets now carry the budget's undivided ten: DefaultRereadOverallLimit {Every: 1s, Burst: 10} and GCPRereadOverallLimit {Every: 4s, Burst: 10}. The architect's ruling is written as the rule it is — the rate divides by the replica count squared because every accepted reread costs a store read on every pod and that is sustained traffic; the burst does not divide at all because what it must admit is one person's write burst, a hard floor fixed in the replica count, while what it guards is a transient on each pod's own writer lock, a soft cost re-bounded immediately by the rate — with the architect's sentence verbatim: one side is a hard floor and the other is a soft cost, and sizing by the soft one is the error this corrects. The floor is recorded as four, not three, with the four rereads named (delete, restore, retag, and the NO_VALUE_KEY retag that expects no-current-value and meets RATE_LIMITED when the bucket is spent) and the tester's measurement quoted: 2 FAIL, 3 FAIL, 4 ok, 5 ok. Ten therefore carries six tokens of headroom at any fleet size, where 10/N put the depth at 3 for a three-pod fleet, under the floor.
proof.negativeControl: The tester measured the floor against the live row with a go build overlay changing only this burst and nothing else, so the refusals it counted are the shared bucket's. The rejected alternative is recorded in the comment so nobody re-proposes it: max(budget/replicas, personWriteBurst) is correct but 10/3 is already under the floor, so from three pods upward the maximum is the floor and the divisor is one nobody uses.

proof.criterion: The architect's acceptance for the comment: the fleet's momentary cost written beside the number at two, three and four pods against the quota the budget cites; the two rules stated apart with their own reasons; the protection written beside the cost; and the direction named without the code acting on it.
proof.surface: The comments themselves, checked by the documentation build that regenerates the broker reference pages from the binaries and validates every internal link.
proof.observed: 43 pages built, all internal links valid, exit 0; check-private-names exit 0 over 4904 files. The momentary cost is stated as the two quantities it is — a burst lets the fleet accept replicas x burst rereads and each costs a store read on every pod, so the store sees replicas squared x burst: 40, 90 and 160 reads at two, three and four pods, twice that in metadata under Secret Manager (80, 180, 320), which against the cited 600 a minute is 8, 18 and 32 seconds of quota — with the sentence that each is a transient spent once and re-bounded by the rate written beside it rather than a paragraph away. One sentence names the direction (the momentary store cost grows with the square of the replica count while the rate is already divided by it, so there is a count beyond which this shape stops making sense, and nobody has had to think about it because the fleet is two) and nothing in the code bounds it: no cap, no guard, no refusal at a replica count, no knob.
proof.negativeControl: cmd/broker-refgen fails the docs build on a BROKER_* variable or route comment it cannot read, and starlight-links-validator on an anchor that does not resolve; the build exits 0 only with both satisfied.

proof.criterion: The architect asked that oauthSecretTimeout's bound be measured rather than pinned: assert the contending call is comfortably inside the timeout, and say what the measured figure was.
proof.surface: The real oauthstore.Store.Secret on a migrated schema of the test's own, driven from two goroutines released together — the exact contention a cold two-pod boot makes on oauth_provider_secret, rather than a process's boot timed from outside.
proof.observed: PASS in 0.24 s, logging '2 pods read the OAuth provider secret at the same moment: 13.99ms and 5.78ms, against oauthSecretTimeout of 10s'. The row asserts the slower of the two returned without error and took less than a quarter of the bound, so it fails only if the margin collapses and never because a runner was slow; no duration is pinned and no process is timed. The constant's comment carries the measurement with its caveat and keeps the reasoning the reviewer asked for: what the call is, that a hang there is a bound socket nobody serves, that meeting the bound exits rather than hangs, and what an operator sees.
proof.negativeControl: The tester's independent measurement of the same contention, psql against a one-row table of the same shape: 2.7-6.3 ms for the contending session and 0.8-1.5 ms for the other over five runs. This row's figures are higher (13.99 ms) because each goroutine's first call also opens its pooled connection, which is the honest reading: both are three orders of magnitude inside a ten-second bound.

packages/envoy/internal/broker/api/handlers_secrets_test.go and packages/envoy/cmd/broker/multiprocess_test.go — one stale burst figure each, in comments; no row, assertion or bound touched
trickyParts: The per-address limit is a derivation and not a constant: RereadLimitFor of the bucket this process mounts. A future reader who turns it back into a constant reintroduces one of the two defects this round fixed — tightening AWS fourfold for a quota it does not use, or leaving one address able to starve a Secret Manager fleet. The tester's row catches it, and it is blind to where the factor comes from.

The two sizing rules are not one rule with two parameters. The rate divides by the replica count squared because it is sustained traffic against a provider's quota; the burst does not divide at all because it is a depth admitting one person's write burst. Anything that treats them alike walks one of them into the other's failure mode, which is exactly what 10/N did.

The burst's floor is four and it is measured, not reasoned: the end-to-end row sends four rereads, the fourth being the NO_VALUE_KEY retag. Tighten the burst and you meet that row; it mounts no bucket of its own and is the burst's only pin.

The invariant assertion is deliberately blind to perAddressFactor and one-sided. A row that recomputes the production formula from the production inputs proves only that arithmetic is deterministic — it would pass at a factor of 0.5, which puts the starve back to one address.
deviations: Two files that hold the tester's rows carry a one-line comment change each: a stale burst figure in handlers_secrets_test.go's rereadsFreely note and in multiprocess_test.go's row 5 premise. Neither is a row, an assertion or a bound, and the diff from the tester's commit shows exactly those two hunks. They were corrected rather than left because a figure restated in prose that nobody updates is the defect class this issue has now fixed five times.

limits_test.go is package api rather than package api_test, because the derivation assertion reads the unexported perAddressFactor and exporting a constant merely to test it would be worse. Its first comment says so.
openQuestions: None. Both tester failures are fixed, the architect's ruling and its three comment requirements are in, the reviewer's three carry-ins and its refusal of the first pin are answered, and no decision is outstanding.
discoveredComplexity: Three figures this round and the last were produced by reasoning and corrected by a measurement or a second reader — an exit status that was always zero, a floor stated as three that measured four, and a fleet transient written as replicas x burst that is replicas squared x burst. All three were wrong in the direction that makes a change look safe. That is a finding about method rather than three slips: in this change, a number nobody measured has been wrong more often than it has been right, and the comments now say which figures are measured and how.

The reviewer's standard is worth carrying: a test that derives the number it is checking from the production inputs proves only that arithmetic is deterministic. The invariant assertion is the one that can fail.
